Manufacturing AI transformation should "start with the smallest closed-loop scenario, first connect data and processes, then layer on AI."

Quality anomaly handling follows a seven-step closed loop of "detect—report—isolate—analyze—correct—verify—close," with the goal of completing the first round of closure within 72 hours.

Detect and report: After frontline staff detect an anomaly, they should report it within 1 hour, recording the product, production line, process step, batch, anomaly type, quantity affected, and detection time, along with on-site photos.

Isolate (contain): Immediately isolate and label work-in-progress and inventory in the affected batch, and if necessary perform 100% inspection of the batch to prevent defective products from escaping; simultaneously assess whether related incoming materials or process steps should be suspended.

Analyze: Organize quality, production, process, procurement, and other relevant parties to conduct root cause analysis, distinguishing direct causes, root causes, and systemic causes.

Correct and verify: Develop corrective actions (CA) and preventive actions (PA), specifying owners and deadlines; after correction, effectiveness must be verified before normal production resumes.

Close and capture: Produce a review report, capture the case and countermeasures in the quality knowledge base, and update the relevant SOPs and inspection standards.

Poka-Yoke makes errors difficult to occur or immediately detectable if they do occur, which is superior to relying on human attention.

[1] (incident-case) Case: Housing scratches and supplier material change
Background: A production line found scratches on a batch of product housings in the assembly process, concentrated in the same batch and coinciding in time with a recent change of housing supplier material.

Investigation: Analyze along two lines. Occurrence side—compare the appearance and material of incoming materials from the old and new suppliers, and send retained samples for testing; also check handling transfer and fixture contact surfaces. Escape side—verify whether the process has appearance inspection and whether limit samples are clear. The results identified the main causes as decreased surface hardness of incoming materials from the new supplier combined with insufficient handling protection, and appearance inspection failed to intercept the defects.

Containment: Isolate and conduct 100% inspection of the batch, and suspend production with the problematic incoming materials.

Correction: Require the supplier to improve according to 8D and tighten incoming inspection; optimize handling transfer containers and protection; add appearance inspection and limit samples to the process; pilot AI visual inspection to improve detection consistency.

Prevention: Incorporate "supplier material changes require PCN + tightened incoming inspection + retained sample comparison" into the standard process and horizontally deploy it to similar production lines.

[2] (qm) Appearance Defect Judgment Standard (Scratches/Stains)
Appearance defects are graded based on defect type, size, location, and quantity.

Scratches: Graded by length and depth. Scratches on Surface A (user-visible surface) longer than 2 mm or deep scratches that can be felt are judged as nonconforming; B/C surfaces are appropriately relaxed. Visual judgment is required under standard lighting (about 1,000 lux), at a specified distance (30 cm), and within a specified time.

Stains/foreign matter: Minor stains that can be wiped off may be reworked; those that cannot be wiped off or are embedded are judged as nonconforming.

Judgment consistency: Limit samples (acceptable/nonconforming boundary samples) should be provided, and inspectors' judgment standards should be calibrated regularly to reduce subjective differences. Introducing AI visual inspection can improve consistency and detection rate, but the model must be calibrated with limit samples.

High-incidence appearance defect stages: Incoming materials, handling and transfer collisions, fixture contact surface wear, and operations.

Root cause analysis must penetrate surface phenomena to identify eliminable root causes.

5 Whys: Continuously ask "why" about the problem, typically reaching the root cause in about 5 layers. Note the need to distinguish two chains: why the defect "occurred," and why the defect "escaped" without being intercepted.

Fishbone diagram (cause-and-effect diagram): Systematically investigate possible causes across six aspects—Man, Machine, Material, Method, Environment, and Measurement (6M). Appearance defects are often related to "Material" (incoming material variation), "Machine/Method" (fixture wear, operating methods), and handling protection.

Criteria for determining the true cause: It can be reproduced with evidence, the problem disappears once eliminated, and it explains why the issue was not previously detected. Avoid treating "human negligence" as a universal conclusion; further ask why processes and error-proofing failed.

Appearance defects are graded based on defect type, size, location, and quantity.

Scratches: Graded by length and depth. Scratches on Surface A (user-visible surface) longer than 2mm or deep scratches that can be felt are judged as nonconforming; B/C surfaces are appropriately relaxed. Visual judgment must be made under standard lighting (about 1,000 lux), at a specified distance (30cm), and within a specified time.

Stains/foreign matter: Minor stains that can be wiped off may be reworked; those that cannot be wiped off or are embedded are judged as nonconforming.

Judgment consistency: Limit samples (acceptable/nonconforming boundary samples) should be provided, and inspectors' judgment criteria should be periodically calibrated to reduce subjective variation. Introducing AI visual inspection can improve consistency and detection rates, but the model must be calibrated with limit samples.

High-incidence stages for appearance defects: incoming materials, handling and transport impacts, fixture contact surface wear, and operator handling.

Manufacturing AI transformation should "start with the smallest closed-loop scenario, first connect data and processes, then layer on AI."

Scenario selection principles: High frequency, clear pain points, quantifiable value, well-defined scope, and easy to demonstrate. Quality incident closure, predictive equipment maintenance, automated production reporting, and process knowledge capture are common first choices.

Implementation path (30/60/90): In 30 days, assess the current state and select a pilot; in 60 days, build an MVP and run a small-scale trial on real data; in 90 days, review and quantify value, then scale up.

Engineering essentials: Data first (collection, integration, unified definitions); AI outputs must be structured, verifiable, and traceable (retain call logs and cited sources); keep humans in the loop, with key decisions confirmed by people; establish evals and observability to continuously monitor cost, latency, and quality.

Common pitfalls: Pursuing a large, all-encompassing platform from the start, neglecting data foundations, and substituting hard-coded results that "look like AI" for genuine capabilities.

质量异常处理遵循「发现—上报—隔离—分析—整改—验证—关闭」七步闭环，目标是在:
Quality incident handling follows the seven-step closed loop of "Detect—Report—Contain—Analyze—Correct—Verify—Close," with the goal of completing the first closure round within 72 hours.

Detect and report: After frontline staff detect an exception, they should report it within 1 hour, recording the product, production line, process step, batch, exception type, affected quantity, and detection time, with on-site photos attached.

Contain (containment): Immediately quarantine and label work-in-progress and inventory from the affected batch, and perform 100% inspection of that batch if necessary to prevent defective outflow; simultaneously assess whether to suspend related incoming materials or process steps.

Analyze: Organize quality, production, process, and procurement stakeholders to conduct root-cause analysis, distinguishing direct causes, root causes, and systemic causes.

Correct and verify: Develop corrective actions (CA) and preventive actions (PA) with clear owners and deadlines; after correction, effectiveness must be verified before normal production resumes.

Close and capture: Produce a review report, capture the case and countermeasures in the quality knowledge base, and update the relevant SOPs and inspection standards.

MES (Manufacturing Execution System) and quality data dashboards make production and quality status visible in real time, forming the foundation for data-driven improvement.

Data integration: Associate ERP, MES, inspection, and equipment data by batch and process step, unify definitions, and eliminate manual aggregation and information silos.

Core dashboards: Real-time output and progress, defect rates and Pareto charts by process step, exception work order status and closure time, equipment utilization rate, and supplier incoming quality pass rate.

Driving improvement: Use Pareto charts to pinpoint high-frequency defect types, measure response efficiency by closure time, and detect abnormal fluctuations with trend alerts.

AI integration: Layer automated exception dispatch, root-cause recommendations, and AI visual inspection results on top of the dashboard to form a digital closed loop of "Detect—Analyze—Resolve—Review."
